speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether the Ministry will look into the process of empanelling specialist doctors to the approved list of insurance companies; (b) what is the Ministry's stand on the violation of medical ethics in the scheme where insurance companies basically reward patients for choosing their panel of doctors; and (c) whether these insurers will be allowed to challenge the opinions of specialists after they had rendered treatment to their patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Health what measures are there to protect Integrated Shield Plan policyholders in the event of an Integrated Shield Plan insurer exiting the market.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether the Ministry actively tracks and compares the itemised bills of Integrated Shield Plan (IP) patients who use public and private healthcare institutions respectively; (b) what strategies has the Ministry embarked on over the last 10 years to address the problem of overtreatment by some doctors; and (c) what role does the Ministry envisage patients playing to address the problem of over-treatment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Health what proportion of Singapore residents are current policyholders of an Integrated Shield Plan (IP) for (i) standard IP for public hospital Class B1 coverage (ii) Class B1 coverage (iii) Class A coverage and (iv) private hospital coverage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: MediShield Life is universal, covers pre-existing conditions and provides basic protection against large healthcare bills.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Excuse me, Senior Minister of State, to confirm, are you taking Questions Nos 24 to 31?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Can I take Questions Nos 24 to 31 together?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If I may continue, Sir, MediShield Life can be used in both public and private healthcare institutions, and coverage is sized to be sufficient for subsidised care.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government provides means-tested subsidies for MediShield Life premiums and MediSave can be used to pay for premiums to keep them affordable.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Individuals may choose to purchase an Integrated Shield Plan, or IP plan, which provides additional benefits beyond MediShield Life to provide more coverage for private healthcare services.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MediSave can be used to pay for IP premiums, subject to withdrawal limits, to help defray the cost of private insurance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In addition, some individuals may also purchase riders on top of their IP plans, if they prefer additional coverage and can afford the premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Riders commonly cover the deductible and co-payments portion of the bill.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Riders are fully private insurance products that must be paid by cash and MediSave withdrawals are not allowed for rider premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Less than half of Singapore residents have riders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In essence, MediShield Life is universal, it is sized to cover the bulk of the large hospital bills for subsidised care.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: IP plans stay right on top of this, to provide for private hospital bills.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And riders go even further on top of the IP plans, to cover for the deductibles and the co-payments.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, you can see it as a three-tier thing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH does track and monitor the bills from both public and private healthcare institutions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Private healthcare costs have been rising rapidly in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In both private and public hospitals, investigations, surgeon fees, treatment services and operating theatre facility fees were key drivers of cost growth for private patients.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In 2016, the Health Insurance Task Force (HITF) comprising members from the Singapore Medical Association (SMA), Life Insurance Association (LIA) Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE), MOH and MAS had recommended various measures, such as panelling and Fee Benchmarks, to help contain claims and healthcare cost escalation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH has been working to implement the HITF recommendations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Fee Benchmarks have been rolled out since 2018, along with appropriate care guidelines.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: One of the recommendations from the HITF was to introduce a minimum co-payment requirement, as IP riders that fully covered deductibles and co-payment had contributed to rising private healthcare cost.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The co-payment ensures what we call "skin in the game", to encourage patients and their doctors to make careful and deliberate decisions on the choice of treatment and the type of care they need.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The IP insurers have also extended this requirement or alternative claims-based pricing from April 2021 to their existing policyholders with riders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While this is not a requirement imposed by MOH, the Ministry supports the move as it will help to encourage appropriate care.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This would mean that bills above $60,000 are capped at $3,000 co-payment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To put things in perspective, less than 3% of inpatient bills in private hospitals today exceed $60,000.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the vast majority of inpatients bills do not actually hit the $3,000 co-payment cap.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This co-payment cap could not be applied to all claims, as it would negate the effect of co-payment once the $3,000 cap was reached.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Take for example, if the co-payment applies to all claims, policyholders may choose a treatment which costs $100,000 instead of another equally effective treatment at $70,000.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is because the policyholder would pay the same amount of $3,000 for either option once they breach the $60,000 limit, where the $3,000 co-payment cap has been reached.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The additional costs would then be borne by the insurer and this eventually translates to higher premiums for other policyholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, the cap was applied to panelled doctors, where there are established fee arrangements to ensure that appropriate and cost-effective treatment is provided.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some have raised concerns with regard to the use of panels.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Questions have been raised on whether limited panel sizes are in the best interest of the patients and whether such practices are anti-competitive in nature or if there are medical ethical concerns around such practices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The use of panels was recommended by the HITF.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Internationally, panels have been used by some countries to keep healthcare costs more predictable, to reduce variation in practices and charging.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These practices do not contravene the Competition Act as any decision to empanel doctors is made by individual insurers independently with the doctors, on mutually acceptable terms.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Such practices do not restrict insurers from competing with one another on their prices, insurance products, or choice of doctors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Nevertheless, MOH has encouraged insurers to make their panel selection criteria more transparent, a move which is also supported by LIA in its "Panel Good Practices Guide" to all insurers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the issue of medical ethics, the Singapore Medical Council's Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines stipulates that doctors should have the best interests of their patient at heart when treating them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This includes prescribing appropriate and cost-effective care that best meets the needs of their patients.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Access to medical care and clinical judgement should therefore not be influenced by empanelment nor any other financial constraints or pressures inherent in any health system.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Should doctors find that the conditions of being on a panel would impose constraints on their ability to care for patients, they may decide for medical ethical reasons to not participate in such panels.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We want to emphasise that patients can make claims for all treatments covered under their IP, regardless of whether the specialist is on the panel or not.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Nonetheless, some doctors have expressed concerns that IP panels do not have an adequate number of specialists, restricting referrals to the appropriate specialist who may not be on the panel, and therefore, limiting the continuity of care.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Patients have also raised concerns that the doctor they are comfortable with, or are familiar with, is not on the panel of their IP insurer and they may not enjoy the additional panel benefits such as the $3,000 co-payment cap.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some have asked insurance panels to be expanded to include all doctors, so long as they do not have a poor track record with the Singapore Medical Council, or SMC.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, some doctors may choose not to be empanelled as they may already have a sufficient pool of patients.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the doctors do have a choice to not be on panels.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is especially the case for areas where there are very few specialists locally.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, MOH encourages IP insurers to enhance their pre-authorisation processes, to give approval for hospitalisation or treatments and their associated costs beforehand.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With pre-authorisation, insurers are able to assess treatments for medical necessity and fee arrangements and appropriateness, including for doctors who are not on their panel.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And patients can also have greater peace of mind knowing that at least a significant portion of their bill will be covered by their IP.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While policyholder benefits may differ, depending on whether they see a panel doctor or a non-panel doctor who is pre-authorised, these benefits should not differ to the extent of prohibiting patients from seeing non-panel doctors or influence patient choices in an undesirable way.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH recognises that some policyholders may wish to switch insurers, whether for more competitive premiums or for better benefits, such as access to more panel doctors, but are unable to do so because of pre-existing conditions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: IPs are commercial products, and their features and pricing are, ultimately, determined by private insurers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, insurers may potentially need to increase the premiums significantly for all policyholders to price in the increased risk they assume for portable IP that covers pre-existing conditions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is why MediShield Life is designed as a scheme to cover all Singaporeans for life with no exclusions and covers all pre-existing conditions to give reassurance to all Singaporeans should they choose to relinquish their private IP plans, for whatever reasons.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Over the last five years, about 5% of IP policyholders relinquished their IP per year on average.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This could be because they may have opted for different coverage, after considering the cost of the premiums, their financial resources and their different healthcare needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Data on the number of policyholders who did not subsequently purchase a new IP or were later admitted to public hospitals is not available.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Consumers should understand their IP terms and conditions when choosing their IPs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Insurers offer policyholders enhanced policy benefits, such as the co-payment cap, lower deductibles or a longer period of pre- and post-hospitalisation coverage for panel treatments.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: All this must be made known to the policyholder prior to policy purchase and at least 30 days before any changes in policyholders' benefits.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Policyholders must be properly advised at the point of purchase or renewal about their coverage, so they can make informed choices about their IP and choice of doctors and care setting.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some have asked if insurers can simply use MOH's Fee Benchmarks to determine all insurance payouts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As Fee Benchmarks are designed to be reasonable ranges of fees for the large majority of cases, insurers can, generally, take reference from the benchmarks for most payouts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Doctors do charge below and above the benchmarks, depending on the nature and the complexity of the cases.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, insurers also need to take into account the medical complexity and specific clinical circumstances, and deviate from the benchmarks for justified and exceptional cases.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: According to LIA, between 5% and 15% of IP claims for surgeon fees were approved above the upper bound of the Fee Benchmarks, depending on the insurer.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Claims scrutiny by insurers may have been perceived as challenging a doctor's professional judgement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Insurers scrutinise claims to ascertain whether treatments were medically necessary and charged appropriately.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This actually protects the interests of policyholders who may otherwise see their insurance premiums rise should claims be paid out indiscriminately.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH recognises that this is an important process for the integrity of the healthcare system and is a common practice internationally.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is, nonetheless, important that the process be handled professionally and efficiently by each insurer.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Insurers should not make the process onerous and ask for unnecessary information unrelated to the claims, imposing a heavy administrative burden on the doctors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The questions and information sought for common conditions can be standardised and streamlined so it will not be perceived as questioning the decisions and judgement of the doctors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If a particular claim is justified, insurers should pay according to the policy benefits.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will be looking more into this issue.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng has raised concerns with the risk of IP insurers exiting the market.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is accomplished through measures, such as establishing regulatory capital requirements and setting corporate governance and risk management requirements and guidance, which are, in turn, reinforced by regular onsite inspections and close engagement with the boards and senior management of insurers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MAS also takes action against insurers whose practices are found to be wanting or where there are breaches of MAS' regulations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: An insurer may decide to exit the IP market because of commercial reasons or due to insolvency.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the event that an insurer exits the IP market, the insurer or the liquidator will seek to arrange for the IP policies to be transferred to another insurer for continuity of coverage.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MAS will ensure that the existing insurer and the insurer taking over the IP policies properly account for policyholders' interests.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The various initiatives covered above will take time to bear fruit.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, we are confident that these measures will help to keep healthcare costs more sustainable.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Looking ahead, the refinement of various IP features will continue to be a multilateral effort between MOH, hospitals, doctors and the insurers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The MHIC comprises representatives from the Academy of Medicine, Singapore (AMS), the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE), the Fee Benchmarks Advisory Committee (FBAC), the Life Insurance Association (LIA), the Singapore Medical Association (SMA), private hospital representatives and with MAS as an observer.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For a start, the Committee will prioritise four specific workstreams.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On this particular last issue, CASE will be leading a sub-committee to the MHIC to deal with the matter comprehensively.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As these issues are complex, some time will be required for the Committee to develop and agree on practical solutions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Processes within the institutions, hospitals and clinics may also have to be adjusted to make it more seamless and streamlined.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MHIC will share its recommendations progressively as they are ready and is working towards a first round of recommendations in the next few months.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The issues surrounding IPs are multi-faceted and require thorough discussions as well as careful balancing of various considerations, to find solutions that best benefit policyholders and patients.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With continued healthy dialogue through the MHIC, MOH will work together with all stakeholders towards developing sustainable solutions for policyholders, payers and providers alike.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The recent public exchange between the Singapore Medical Association and the Life Insurance Association of Singapore has put into focus the role of the regulator, namely, MOH.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even as I acknowledge the Senior Minister of State's establishment of the MHIC, which has been set up to look into some of these issues, I have, nonetheless, two supplementary questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second supplementary question is in conjunction with the first, which is, together with the establishment of the database, would MOH, as regulator, consider setting up an independent panel of assessors under its purview which would be accessible to patients, doctors and insurers to resolve disputes about fees and the necessity of medical procedures?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In fact, these two items are already being done.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The first, on the database for bill sizes, when we have the Fee Benchmarks Advisory Committee, in fact, the database on fees that are charged across a diverse range of procedures across various institutions are already available for the Committee, which comprises practitioners and insurers, to collectively deliberate on what the kind of benchmarking ought to be.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, yes, the database is available and I think that will provide some scrutiny by the relative stakeholders to ensure that, whether it is payouts or benchmarking, they are considered fair to the policyholders and to the payers as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Limiting the choice of doctors for patients and insured individuals, personally, I feel that, definitely, this is to the disadvantage of the patient.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I cannot understand how this is not anti-competitive.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Limiting choice to the patient will limit the patient's ability in terms of choosing the right doctors, unless you are telling me that the panel itself comprises more than 50% of all doctors in Singapore, to make sure that each insurer must have a certain percentage of doctors on it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With the Fee Benchmarks in place, can we then remove the panel completely?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That is something that we have to consider.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last of all, I also wish to echo the question by the Leader of the Opposition whether MOH will be coming up with a ranking of the insurers because MOH will be seen as a neutral party, that is, in order to protect the consumer.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The issue of whether the limited size of panels of certain insurers, as I have said in my reply, it will be very difficult to say that we make the panels include 100% of all doctors, because doctors have a choice not to be on panels as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With pre-authorisation, the doctor puts in his diagnosis, gives a certain quote on the treatment cost that is needed and the insurer has a chance to see whether this cost is fair and whether the type of treatment that is proposed is reasonable for the kind of diagnosis that is being put forth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In that sense, the patient can then have access to any doctor, subject to a pre-authorisation, if they are not on the panel.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is a mechanism that is already available today.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But, what we need to do is to make sure that the process is much more streamlined and seamless, so that there is not too much administrative burden on the clinics and the patient does not have to wait too long for this process to be completed before they can have access to care by a different doctor, by a different specialist.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is very hard to say which insurer ranks number one or which is ranked at the bottom because they may have product differentiation that meets different persons' needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And for a person where the product meets his needs, it could be number one, as an insurer, but if the other product meets the other person's needs better, that could be number one in the other person's eyes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think it is very hard for MOH to decide from one person to the next which is the best product to suit the person's needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: What we should do is to put more information so that patients and policyholders can make the right informed choices.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On the issue of patient voices, Mr Deputy Speaker, can the Senior Minister of State assure us that MOH's proposed dispute resolution mechanism will actively involve the patient's perspective and the journey experienced by patients, whether as existing policyholders navigating the IP system or potential policyholders or former policyholders who may feel excluded.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My Clementi residents who are on Integrated Shield plans (IPs), some of them, they tell me of the challenges involved in making a claim, despite having been with the same firm for many years, despite the full support of the doctor looking after them, whether the doctor is in the private or public sector.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On the second question, Mr Deputy Speaker, that of the bargaining power of patients, policyholders and consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Senior Minister of State earlier spoke about the scenario of what happens if an IP insurer exits the market.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He said that there would be a negotiation or discussion between the agencies and the insurance provider about ensuring that patients are covered.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But I ask the Ministry, in the event of an IP insurer exiting the market, is there a mechanism to ensure that patients who already have existing conditions will be appropriately covered and recognised in a way that does not disadvantage them if the insurer exits the market?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I furthermore would like to ask MOH, whether MOH would consider establishing some kind of regulatory backstop to protect patients?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because once you have a mechanism in policy to protect patients when an insurer exits the market, to allow these patients to transit in a way that is non-discriminatory, not unfavourable, to another insurer, I put it to the Ministry that that can be the beginning of a mechanism to allow patients to transition between insurers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I suggest to the Ministry that once patients have the option of transiting with the potential for having pre-existing conditions covered to some extent, as is the case in other regulatory jurisdictions like Australia, there is better bargaining power for the consumer and that leads to a better functioning market as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: His first question pertains to patient voices should there be a dispute by the policyholder against the insurer and what mechanisms are there today to address some of these grievances.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, FIDReC is a mechanism that is already available.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But we do feel that with better patient and public education, that will raise the awareness of consumers' rights and when they think that their rights, under the policy terms, have been violated.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So better patient education, better policyholder education is another important thrust to get this done.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We welcome the fact that CASE will be forming a sub-committee under the MHIC to further study this issue, and also to look at how they can better represent the voices of consumers, policyholders and patients.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The second issue is about what would happen if the insurers were to exit the financial sector.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The PPF Scheme does not merely provide compensation of crystallised claims when an insurer fails, but also seeks to ensure continuity where possible for the effective policyholders in the event of an insurance failure.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, you could also fund a transfer or run-off of the IP portfolio business to another IP insurer to ensure continuity of coverage for the affected policyholders, if necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In Singapore, what is useful for Singaporean citizens, is to always know at the back of their minds that they have a safety net called MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I just have one supplementary question, which is whether this method of empanelling doctors will impact patients, who may need to change doctors halfway during their treatment for whatever reasons?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Once we can get a more seamless and streamlined, pre-authorisation process, it effectively opens up access to care by all doctors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And the patient, then do not have to really worry so much about whether doctors are panelled or non-panelled.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, at the moment, there is actually no restriction of care, but there is some friction in the process.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With pre-authorisation, hopefully we can make this much more seamless and reduce a lot more anxiety for patients going for treatment, when they have to go beyond a panel to access a specialist outside the panel.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I hope that will help Members understand that the MHIC will prioritise this as one of the key streams they want to work at.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This points to a rather high proportion of voluntary downgrading by patients, meaning that they are eligible to seek treatment in private hospitals but end up going to public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does the Senior Minister of State think that Singaporeans are over insured for private insurance, which they do not use?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And secondly, other plans to better educate Singaporeans about their options of different Integrated Shield Plans, so they do not get all the information from insurance agents who are trying to sell them private hospital plans?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And of course, CASE can play a stronger role in patient and policyholder education as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I think, for his first question, he is conflicting two different numbers together which do not quite necessarily gel.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Just because there are only 17% of hospital beds, it does not mean 40% of people cannot buy insurance for private sector.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It does not mean that everybody who buys a policy, gets sick and gets admitted to the hospital all at the same time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is a choice to buy, it does not necessarily mean that they will necessarily have to consume.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It does not necessarily mean that the size of the number of beds we have should then limit the amount of policy coverage a particular segment of population goes for.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I hope that helps him to understand why the numbers should not necessarily be conflicted together.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, please make it a very short supplementary; then, we will move on to the next topic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: I want to put on record as a declaration that I am a medical doctor, looking after patients in the public sector, for avoidance of ambiguity.
